title: Fats & Oils
subtitle: Before 8000 BC · Bone Grease, Fat Lamps, the First Pots and the Hunter’s Fat

entries.label: Fat as the hunter’s target, and perhaps a reason to domesticate
entries.loc: The Aleutians and the American Plains
entries.hint: Kiple notes that selection for the fattest animals is documented in the preference of prehistoric Aleut hunters for sea lions, the largest and fattiest sea mammals, and in the bison remains from archaeological sites, which show selection of the fattest individuals. Domestic animals store more fatty tissue than their wild ancestors, which may have been a further incentive to keep them.
entries.note: CONTEXT (an argument in an encyclopedia chapter): Kiple (2000) the introduction on food and subsistence (PDF pp.93–95), citing Yesner 1988, Denniston 1972 and Armitage 1986. The date is a placeholder for the end of the Ice Age; the Aleut and bison remains are not dated in the passage.

entries.label: Lean meat is not enough: the explorers’ accounts of “protein poisoning”
entries.loc: North America and East Africa, explorers’ accounts
entries.hint: Speth gathers explorers’ and travellers’ accounts of what living on lean meat does to people. A Canadian expedition of 1863 found it nearly as hard to live on dried lean meat without grease as to starve; in East Africa the members of a later expedition wrote that they craved fat as eagerly as the Eskimo, found African game very lean, and prized the humps of oxen; and hippopotamus fat boiled down to something very like pork lard. His chapters ‘Excess protein and the importance of fat’ and ‘Historic accounts of protein poisoning’ use such accounts to argue that lean meat alone cannot sustain foragers, which gives the hunter’s pull to fat (th1), bone grease (te1, ec4) and marrow (ec2) their reason.
entries.note: CONTEXT (book read, an argument from 18th and 19th-century accounts): Speth, The Paleoanthropology and Archaeology of Big-Game Hunting: Protein, Fat, or Politics? (2010), ch.4, PDF pp.87–101 (Palliser 1863; von Höhnel on Africa). The date is a placeholder for the end of the Ice Age; the accounts are recent, and the inference to the Palaeolithic is Speth’s.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Marrow and gazelle grease, wild olives and nuts, shellfish and Nile fish, and fish in the first pots

entries.label: Pinnacle Point: shellfish, and perhaps beached-whale blubber, about 164,000 years ago
entries.loc: Pinnacle Point, Mossel Bay, South Africa
entries.hint: The sea cave of Pinnacle Point 13B on South Africa’s south coast, dated by luminescence to 164 ± 12 thousand years ago, shows that humans had by then widened their diet to include marine resources, perhaps in response to the cold, dry conditions of that glacial stage; the authors suggest shellfish may have been crucial to the survival of these early humans. Among the shellfish is a fragment of a whale barnacle, tentatively identified as Coronula diadema, which the paper says suggests scavenging of beached whale blubber and skin with attached barnacles. Scraped hematite, probably for red pigment, and bladelet tools come from the same layers.
entries.note: ANCHOR (paper read): Marean et al., ‘Early human use of marine resources and pigment in South Africa during the Middle Pleistocene’, Nature 449 (2007) pp.905–908. The blubber reading is the authors’ tentative suggestion from one barnacle fragment, not a residue result; shellfish themselves are low in fat, so the fat link rests on the whale alone.

entries.label: Wild olive stones heaped in Palaeolithic and Neolithic sites
entries.hint: Hints of the first human uses of the wild olive, the oleaster, are scattered through the Palaeolithic and Neolithic layers across the Mediterranean: from Spain and the French Riviera to North Africa, the Greek islands and Israel, archaeologists have found heaps of oleaster pits that suggest the fruit was being collected. These show gathering, not pressing; the evidence for a cultivated tree begins in the Chalcolithic Levant.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; no sites or dates named): Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011), the opening chapter. The range is the ‘Paleolithic and Neolithic’ of his sentence, not a dating. See fats-8000bc-1200bc::ec2 for the domesticated olive.

entries.label: Ohalo II: wild olives, almonds and pistachios among the oldest plant remains
entries.hint: The waterlogged site of Ohalo II on the Sea of Galilee, dated to about 23,000 years ago near the height of the last glaciation, preserved more than 90,000 plant remains from 142 taxa. Grass seeds seem to have been the staple, supplemented by Mount Tabor oak acorns, almonds, pistachios, wild olives and fruits and berries, and grinding and pounding stones were in use. Nothing in the sources found shows that oil was pressed from the nuts or the olives; they are fat-bearing foods gathered, as at ec3.
entries.note: SECONDARY (news and university pages and the abstract of a 2004 PNAS paper, PMC470712, found by web search; not read in full): the ‘fat-bearing’ reading is the folio’s, since the sources describe the nuts and olives as food, not as oil sources.

entries.label: Gazelle bones broken for marrow and grease in the Levantine Epipalaeolithic
entries.loc: Northern Israel, the southern Levant and Jordan
entries.hint: A taphonomic study of five gazelle assemblages from northern Israel links bone fragmentation and survival to fat yield, and concludes that intensive marrow and grease extraction was the main factor shaping which gazelle bones survived, at a roughly steady intensity through the period. Measurements of fresh mountain gazelle carcasses found the most marrow in spring and less fat in early autumn, yet marrow was a reliable, if small, fat resource in every season, and the foragers preferred the bones with the best marrow yield. At Shubayqa 6 in Jordan, at the Late Natufian to Pre-Pottery Neolithic A transition, fire-cracked basalt and burnt, fragmented bones suggest grease was extracted on a large scale.
entries.note: SECONDARY (abstracts and catalogue listings found by web search; the papers not read): Munro & Bar-Oz (2005) on five northern Israeli gazelle assemblages; Bar-Oz & Munro (2007) on marrow yields of mountain gazelle; the Shubayqa 6 excavation reports. The ‘Epipalaeolithic’ bracket is supplied from general knowledge, since the abstracts give the period name, not the dates. The Natufian volume read since (Bar-Yosef & Valla, eds., 2013, PDF pp.144, 147, 151) confirms the practice in the bone itself: at el-Wad Terrace, cut marks, percussion marks and spiral fractures show skinning, dismemberment, roasting and marrow extraction, and gazelle long bones were routinely cracked for marrow.

entries.label: Nile fishers at Wadi Kubbaniya: fish processed on the dunes at the flood
entries.hint: The Late Palaeolithic camps at Wadi Kubbaniya, north-west of Aswan, were used during the Nile floods, and fish bones are common in the occupation layers beside those of wild cattle, hartebeest, birds and the occasional hippopotamus; one excavation report argues that fish exploitation may have been a major part of the subsistence pattern, with plant processing minor, and links the site to fish processing and perhaps storage. No fat or oil is reported: the fat of the catch is the folio’s inference.
entries.note: CONTEXT (excavation summaries and a Metropolitan Museum essay found by web search; not read in full): the 17,000–15,000 BC bracket is the Museum’s; a later site there (WK26) has a radiocarbon date of 12,060 BP. Egypt is filed under the Near East in the atlas though the site is African.

entries.label: Amur River pots cook fish oils on the lower river and ruminant fat on the middle
entries.loc: The Amur River, Russian Far East
entries.hint: Lipid analysis of 28 sherds from sites on the lower Amur (Khummi, Gasya, Goncharka 1) and the middle Amur (Gromatukha), dated about 16,200 to 10,200 years ago, found that the lower-river pots were used to process aquatic oils, probably of salmonids and freshwater fish, as in Japan, while the Gromatukha vessels showed a significant share of lipids from ruminant animals. The two pottery traditions also differ in how the pots were made. The authors note that Late Glacial hunter-gatherers began to use ceramic cooking vessels in three separate regions of East Asia: China, Japan and the Russian Far East.
entries.note: ANCHOR (paper read): Shoda et al., ‘Late Glacial hunter-gatherer pottery in the Russian Far East: indications of diversity in origins and use’, Quaternary Science Reviews (2020). The region’s acidic soils leave little other evidence of diet, as the authors say. Compare ec1 for Japan.

entries.label: Japan’s Incipient Jōmon cooks boil fish and sea animals in the world’s earliest pots
entries.hint: Lipids recovered from charred deposits on Incipient Jōmon pottery of about 15,000 to 11,800 years ago show that most of the pots were used to process freshwater and marine organisms: of 101 deposits across Japan’s main islands, isotope values point to high-trophic-level aquatic food. The authors suggest that productive waters may have prompted the investment in pottery. A later study of about 800 vessels links early pottery with intensified fishing, first of salmon and then of a wider range including shellfish and marine mammals.
entries.note: SECONDARY (abstracts and university news found by web search; papers not read): Craig et al., ‘Earliest evidence for the use of pottery’, Nature 496 (2013) pp.351–354; University of York news of 2018 on about 800 vessels. Residues show aquatic foods were cooked; they do not isolate marine fat as such.

entries.label: Hunters crack bones for marrow and boil out grease: akutuk and pemmican
entries.loc: The Arctic and the Great Plains, recorded practice
entries.hint: Northern hunting peoples’ recorded practice shows what an early fat economy looked like. Caribou are lean except for fat round the viscera, under the skin and in the marrow; the ends of the long bones are smashed for marrow, and the fragments boiled to make ‘bone juice’. Inuit informants prized marrow for its low-melting-point oleic acid. Marrow and back-fat go into akutuk, ‘Eskimo ice cream’, with berries and snow; on the Plains, hot liquid marrowfat poured over pulverised jerky and sealed in a hide sack was pemmican, from Cree pimikân, grease.
entries.note: CONTEXT (recorded practice of recent peoples, not a Palaeolithic find): Kiple (2000) the caribou-hunting chapter (PDF p.521, after Binford 1978 and Spiess 1979) and the pemmican passage in the cattle chapter (PDF p.488). The date is a placeholder for the end of the Ice Age; the antiquity of the method is shown only by sites such as te1.

entries.label: Mongongo nuts and eland fat: the fats of the Kalahari San
entries.loc: The Kalahari, Botswana and Namibia, recorded practice
entries.hint: Richard Lee’s study of the !Kung San records the mongongo nut as a staple supplying at least half of the vegetable diet by weight; its kernel is about 58 per cent fat, some 600 calories per 100 g, and with the baobab nut and tsin bean it supplies fats that substitute for meat when game is scarce. Yet animal fat is ‘one of the elements most scarce in the San diet’: underground animals such as warthogs are prized because they are fat, the marrow in the jawbones of large animals is a highly valued food, and eland fat is a very highly valued gift, eaten and rubbed on the body and on implements.
entries.note: CONTEXT (ethnography of the 1960s–70s, not an archaeological find): Lee & DeVore (eds.), Kalahari Hunter-Gatherers (1976), Lee’s chapter, PDF pp.58–60, 72 and 386; the fat figure is read from his table of the composition of San wild foods. The date is a placeholder for the end of the Ice Age. The forest of the San’s ancestors cannot be assumed to have had the same foods.

entries.label: Avocado stones in four countries by 9000 BC: the fruit-fat of the Americas
entries.hint: Avocado stones dating between 11,000 and 9,000 years ago have been found at Huaca Prieta in Peru, San Isidro in Colombia, El Gigante in Honduras and Coxcatlán in Mexico. They give early evidence of a mutualism between people and relict avocado stands, in a tree whose seeds had been spread through the Pleistocene by megafauna and whose wild populations run from Mexico to South America. Kiple adds the context of fat: with so few domesticated animals in the New World, many Americans took their fat from the avocado.
entries.note: ANCHOR (article read) for the finds and dates; SECONDARY for the fat: VanDerwarker et al., ‘Early evidence of avocado domestication from El Gigante Rockshelter, Honduras’, PNAS 122 (2025) e2417072122, introduction (PDF p.2); Kiple (2000) introduction to Part II p.73 (PDF p.110). The article does not discuss fat, so the fat clause is Kiple’s.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Rendering bone grease, burning fat for light, and the first pots

entries.label: Neanderthals render bone grease at Neumark-Nord, about 125,000 years ago
entries.hint: At Neumark-Nord 2 in central Germany, beside a lake in an interglacial about as warm as today, Neanderthals crushed the bones of at least 172 large mammals — horses, deer, aurochs — into tens of thousands of fragments and heated them in water to render bone grease. A 2025 study calls it the earliest clear case of intensive grease rendering in the Palaeolithic: signs of such intensification had been thought to begin at Upper Palaeolithic sites about 28,000 years ago, long after Neanderthals had gone. More than 16,500 flint artefacts and traces of fire mark a place that was organised and returned to.
entries.note: SECONDARY (university press releases and popular coverage of one paper, found by web search; the paper not read): Kindler et al., Science Advances (2025), on Neumark-Nord 2. The ‘fat factory’ framing and the idea that grease offset a protein-heavy diet are interpretations in the coverage, not findings. Compare fats-8000bc-1200bc::te1, which holds only Kiple’s undated remark that rendering was the first extraction method.

entries.label: Stone lamps burn animal fat: Lascaux and the Upper Palaeolithic
entries.loc: Dordogne, France, and other Palaeolithic caves
entries.hint: The French Ministry of Culture’s account of Lascaux counts over a hundred lamps in the cave, most of them limestone plates with a hollow centre to hold the fuel, and one red sandstone lamp with a handle and an engraving. Analysis of samples from some lamps identified fatty acids of animal origin, and the wicks were conifer and non-woody. Not every ‘lamp’ was one: of 302 artefacts examined in one study only 85 were confirmed as lamps, and burn marks are rare before the Magdalenian. An experiment of 1981 found that animal fat sets hard again when the lamp is out, which suits a portable light.
entries.note: SECONDARY (French Ministry of Culture Lascaux page, a 2002 Bulletin de la Société préhistorique française article and an experimental study of 1981, seen through a web search; not read in full): the 40,000-year start comes from a hobbyist page citing de Beaune & White 1993 and is the loosest part of the bracket; the confirmed-lamp count is de Beaune 1987 as a Spanish cave paper reports it.

entries.label: The first pots in China, about 20,000 years ago
entries.hint: Pottery from Xianrendong Cave, dated to about 20,000 years ago, at the peak of the last ice age, was made by mobile foragers and is 2,000 or more years older than other pottery known in East Asia. Many sherds bear burning on the outside, scorch and soot that point to cooking, and the authors note that cooking in pots allows energy gains from starch-rich food as well as meat. They list residue and starch analyses of such early sherds as work still to be done, so what the pots held, and whether any fat went into them, is not known; boiling bones for grease, as in te1, is possible in such a pot but not shown.
entries.note: CONTEXT (paper read): Wu et al., ‘Early Pottery at 20,000 Years Ago in Xianrendong Cave, China’, Science 336 (2012) pp.1696–1700, with its remark that residue analyses of Xianrendong and other Late Pleistocene Chinese sherds remain to be made. The grease clause is the folio’s inference.
